overview: Bukhara’s state linked oasis towns, irrigated farms and caravan routes in Central Asia. The map’s “Bukara” entry covers 1530 to 1600, during Shaybanid rule; “Bokhara” covers 1878 to 1900, during the Manghit emirate under Russian protection. They represent different phases, not one unchanging dynasty. Both imported outlines miss Bukhara city: the earlier one lies too far east, the later one too far south. Their dates are map coverage, not the state’s lifetime.

periods.title: Shaybanid Bukhara
periods.summary: Bukhara became a major center of Uzbek dynastic power and patronage.

periods.title: Janid rulers
periods.summary: A new dynasty governed amid changing relations with powerful local and tribal leaders.

periods.title: Manghit ascendancy
periods.summary: Manghit ministers became rulers; Shah Morad adopted the amir’s title in 1785.

periods.title: Russian protection
periods.summary: After military defeat, the emirate retained its ruler but lost independent foreign policy.

items.text: Property records from the mid-sixteenth-century Molla Amiri Mosque quarter name grocers, a shoemaker, a grain broker, a bath attendant and a cart driver. They bring ordinary occupations into view beside rulers: a neighborhood needed shoes repaired and grain delivered as well as government.

The same neighborhood included streets named for mats and rope-makers. These occupational clues come from documents about people and property, rather than a modern reconstruction of a perfect bazaar. Shops and workshops were part of the city’s residential fabric.

Water helped organize Bukhara’s geography. Districts followed major canals, while smaller quarters were commonly associated with a mosque and a communal reservoir; one reservoir could serve several quarters. A water source was therefore a shared neighborhood responsibility, not simply a private household possession.

In 1585 Abdullah Khan’s delegation to the Mughal emperor Akbar brought horses, camels, garments and prized pigeons, together with a specialist pigeon-handler. Diplomacy also advertised valuable goods. Even a bird could travel with its own expert companion.

Bukhara’s covered commercial buildings included Taki Sarafon, the Dome of the Moneychangers, and Taki Tilpak Furushan, associated with headgear sellers. Their names preserve different kinds of commercial work. The historic city was a network of markets, routes and monumental crossroads, not just a collection of royal buildings.

For 1848, the heritage evaluation records thirty-eight caravanserais and sixteen public baths in Bukhara, alongside bazaars and trading arcades. Visitors needed lodging, and urban residents had institutions for washing. These counts describe that nineteenth-century city, not every settlement or every earlier century.

Under the Manghit rulers, Bukhara attracted students from across Central Asia. Historical estimates count roughly ten thousand students among its many madrasas, though the number of institutions varies by source. Islamic learning gave the city influence beyond the territory its amirs directly controlled.

The wealthy Juybari family endowed schools, mosques, canals, bridges and caravanserais. Surviving purchase records and endowment deeds show property income being assigned to maintain institutions and pay their employees. Buildings needed continuing revenue: a splendid opening ceremony could not fund centuries of repairs by itself.

Ay Padshah Bibi’s name and seal appear on endowment deeds. In 1671 she provided madrasas and a water tank on the street of Abd al-Aziz Khan’s mosque. The written record preserves a woman’s substantial public patronage even where the buildings themselves have disappeared.

In the sixteenth-century Bukhara book workshop of Abd al-Aziz Khan, the calligrapher Mir Hosayn Kolangi worked with other scribes. He helped copy four works by Jami in 1548 to 1549; that manuscript is now Chester Beatty Per 213. A finished book could be a coordinated team achievement.

An early nineteenth-century embroidered cover at the Metropolitan Museum is attributed to Bukhara. Such suzanis decorated homes and formed part of a bride’s dowry. The museum’s example has silk embroidery on linen, with bold flowers along its border and more delicate curling stems inside.

The museum describes a usual suzani technique: a specialist drew a design across loosely joined strips, which were separated for the bride’s relatives to embroider and then sewn together again. Slight mismatches at the seams could reveal shared handiwork. Family teamwork did not always produce perfect alignment.

A gold coin struck for Nasr Allah at Bukhara in the Islamic year 1257 weighs 4.55 grams in Charles Torrey’s catalogue. Its border includes an interlaced dotted design. The date, mint inscription and measured metal turn a tiny object into evidence for nineteenth-century monetary production.

In the later emirate, promises of reform did not necessarily bring reform. Alim Khan announced changes against corruption and in education but generally followed conservative policies. Young Bukharan reformers challenged the regime. Debates about schools were part of a larger struggle over who could change public life.

After losing his throne, Alim Khan wrote a Persian account of Bukhara’s suffering. Its text is dated 1921, but the surviving edition includes a map with information after 1925. A former ruler’s memoir is valuable evidence of his perspective; it is not a neutral account of everyone’s experience.

“ضرب بخارا” means “struck at Bukhara.” This short mint phrase is printed in Torrey’s transcription of Nasr Allah’s gold coin dated AH 1257, from the nineteenth-century emirate. It uses the Arabic script employed for Persian. Here writing identified where money was made, rather than telling a long royal story.

ending.text: The emirate survived the map’s 1900 endpoint. The Red Army overthrew Alim Khan in September 1920, ending Manghit rule; he went into exile. A new Bukharan republic replaced the monarchy. The city’s inhabitants, languages, religious traditions and crafts continued through profound political change.
